actions.justification: Mandatory first step — continuous monitoring of HR, BP, SpO2, and RR to establish baseline and detect hemodynamic instability, which guides PE risk stratification.

Mandatory — Wells score is the validated clinical prediction rule for PE probability. Pleuritic chest pain and acute dyspnea are key Wells criteria. Result determines need for D-dimer vs. direct CT-PA.

Mandatory — D-dimer is the first-line diagnostic test for PE in patients with low-to-moderate pre-test probability. A negative high-sensitivity D-dimer effectively rules out PE without further imaging.

12-lead ECG is a Class I recommendation for acute chest pain and should be obtained within 10 minutes of first medical contact to evaluate for STEMI or other ST changes. This patient presents with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain.

Supplemental oxygen should be administered as a supportive measure for a patient with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain while diagnostic workup proceeds, even with SpO2 of 98% to maintain adequate oxygenation.

Chest X-ray is indicated in the initial assessment of acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain to evaluate for alternative diagnoses (pneumothorax, pneumonia, pleural effusion) and is part of PE workup per guidelines.
Echocardiogram can assess for right heart strain, which is important in suspected pulmonary embolism presenting with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain, helping risk-stratify the patient.

Given acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain with Wells score and D-dimer already ordered, CT pulmonary angiography is the definitive imaging to confirm or exclude pulmonary embolism per PE guidelines.

A 12-lead ECG should be obtained per AHA guidelines for acute chest pain to evaluate for STEMI, right heart strain (S1Q3T3 pattern suggesting PE), or other arrhythmias. Note: order_ecg was done but order_imaging_ecg is a distinct available action.
Pulmonology consultation is appropriate given suspected pulmonary embolism presentation with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain to assist with further management decisions.

ABG is indicated to assess oxygenation, ventilation, and acid-base status in a patient with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain (suspected PE). Provides objective data on hypoxemia and A-a gradient to support diagnosis and severity assessment.

Lower extremity venous duplex ultrasound is indicated to evaluate for DVT as a source of suspected pulmonary embolism. Identifying proximal DVT supports PE diagnosis and guides anticoagulation decisions per PE workup guidelines.

Echocardiogram is indicated to assess for right heart strain, which would indicate hemodynamically significant PE and guide risk stratification (massive vs submassive PE), informing decisions about thrombolysis or advanced interventions.
CBC to evaluate for anemia, infection, or thrombocytosis which may contribute to or complicate suspected PE/pulmonary embolism workup.
BMP to assess renal function (relevant if contrast used for CT-PA), electrolytes, and metabolic status in this patient with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain.
BNP to assess for right heart strain or heart failure as part of risk stratification in suspected pulmonary embolism.
Troponin is indicated to assess for right heart strain in suspected PE, which can indicate severity and guide management decisions.
Coagulation studies (PT/INR, aPTT) are needed prior to initiating anticoagulation therapy for suspected PE to establish baseline and guide dosing.
Lactate helps assess for tissue hypoperfusion and can assist in risk stratification of PE severity (massive vs submassive).

Patient presents with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain, with CT-PA and D-dimer ordered, highly suspicious for pulmonary embolism. Per PE guidelines, empiric anticoagulation should be initiated when clinical suspicion is high (Wells score assessed) while awaiting confirmatory imaging results. Patient is hemodynamically stable (HR 80, BP 120/80, SpO2 98%), making anticoagulation the appropriate next step. No contraindications identified.

Patient with likely pulmonary embolism (acute dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, extensive PE workup completed) should receive LMWH as definitive therapeutic anticoagulation. This is the guideline-recommended treatment for hemodynamically stable PE.

Consult interventional radiology as a precautionary measure for potential catheter-directed thrombolysis or embolectomy if the patient deteriorates or if CT-PA confirms significant clot burden, per PE management guidelines.

Patient has suspected/confirmed PE with stable hemodynamics. Unfractionated heparin (UFH) is a standard anticoagulation option for PE per guidelines, and initiating/continuing heparin infusion is appropriate as part of ongoing anticoagulation management for this patient.

Patient with suspected PE (pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea) who has received anticoagulation. IV fluid support may be appropriate if right heart strain develops. Vitals are currently stable (HR 80, BP 120/80, SpO2 98%), but cautious IV fluid administration can support RV preload. This is the most clinically appropriate optional action available given the completed workup and ongoing assessment phase.
